power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: In the past two decades, research has indicated that variation in the course of mental disorders may be partially explained by interpersonal heterogeneity.
Patients with interpersonal different styles can have variable outcomes even when they do not differ in pre-treatment symptom presentation or psychiatric diagnosis.
This phenomenon is known as interpersonal pathoplasticity.

In this paper we present the results of a systematic review of 19 studies conducted in adult patients with DSM-IV Axis I mental disorders that (a) used the Inventory of Interpersonal Problems to identify subgroups of patients with similar interpersonal styles, and (b) compared these interpersonal subgroups in terms of demographic and clinical characteristics (e.g., age, symptom severity) and course over time (e.g., therapeutic alliance development).
Across diagnostic categories, we found few differences between subgroups in demographics and in clinical presentation.
At the same time, there were subgroup differences in the course of mental disorder.

Specifically, having a warm-submissive interpersonal style tended to be more favourable for treatment than having a cold-submissive or cold-dominant style, in support of interpersonal pathoplasticity.
This phenomenon has transdiagnostic potential in clinical practice, since between-person variation in interpersonal style provides opportunities for improving and tailoring treatment.
However, our review primarily included studies on patients diagnosed with anxiety and mood disorders.

To find additional evidence for interpersonal pathoplasticity, future studies should assess interpersonal heterogeneity in patients with other mental disorders and examine its relation to the course of these disorders.
Interactions between patients and clinicians are shaped by each person's interpersonal style, that is, the behavioural pattern the person generally uses to interact with others.

Interpersonal style can be defined by a blend of communion, representing motivations to connect and get along with others, and agency, representing motivations to separate from and get ahead of others (Wright et al., 2023).

text.text: This agency-communion framework, also known as the Rose of Leary (1957) or interpersonal circumplex model (Fournier et al., 2010), has been used within the clinical sciences and beyond (Eriksson, 2018; Girard et al., 2017; Kurt and Frimer, 2015; Markey et al., 2005).

text.text: This review focused on between-person variation in interpersonal style among patients diagnosed with a mental disorder and aimed to show how this may relate to the presentation and course of their symptoms.
The interpersonal circumplex model is central to Contemporary Integrative Interpersonal Theory (CIIT; Wright et al., 2023).

text.text: Rooted in classic interpersonal theory (Sullivan, 1953) and building on the work of Leary (1957) and various others (e.g., Horowitz, 2004; Kiesler, 1996), CIIT holds that a person's interpersonal style is shaped by their social development, is expressed more in some social contexts than in others, and may cause interpersonal problems if it does not match the present social environment for a longer period of time.

text.text: These problems can become a source of distress and may thereby contribute to a deterioration of mental health.

Indeed, currently symptomatic patients diagnosed with a mental disorder generally report high levels of interpersonal distress (e.g., Gómez Penedo et al., 2025a; Harrison et al., 2022; McEvoy et al., 2013).

text.text: However, the association between a diagnosis and an interpersonal style is complex.
Two patients with different diagnoses may have the same interpersonal style (Girard et al., 2017).

text.text: This is consistent with the multifinality principle of developmental psychopathology, which holds that the same risk factor can have different outcomes (Cicchetti and Rogosch, 1996).

text.text: Conversely, in line with the equifinality principle, which holds that different risk factors can have the same outcome, two patients with the same mental disorder may have different interpersonal styles.

For example, while some patients with social phobia (social anxiety disorder) tend to be low in agency and low in communion, others may tend to be low in agency in combination with high communion (Cain et al., 2010).

text.text: While the former group will primarily report being socially avoidant (i.e., problems with cold submissiveness) the latter group will primarily report being overly accommodating (i.e., problems with warm submissiveness).
The Inventory of Interpersonal Problems (IIP) was developed by Horowitz et al. (1988) and can be used to gain insight into levels of interpersonal distress and into respondents' interpersonal style.

text.text: The IIP includes typical interpersonal behaviours and asks how hard respondents find it to do these behaviours (e.g., "say no to other people") or to what extent respondents do them too much (e.g., "please other people").

text.text: Results from these studies have been used to argue that while these interpersonal subgroups are largely comparable in terms of clinical presentation (e.g., anxiety or depression symptom severity, diagnostic comorbidity) before treatment, they may show different trajectories in the course of their disorder and vary substantially in treatment outcome (in terms of reduction in both symptoms and interpersonal distress; Cain et al., 2010; Salzer et al., 2011).

text.text: Thus, interpersonal heterogeneity might contribute to between-patient differences in clinical outcomes.
This notion, that interpersonal style accounts for variation in the course of mental disorder, is known as interpersonal pathoplasticity (Wright et al., 2023).

text.text: The fact that two patients diagnosed with the same mental disorder can vary substantially in their clinical outcome remains a major problem in clinical practice.

While this may be explained by between-patient heterogeneity in symptom severity and presentation (e.g., Wienicke et al., 2023), it might also be explained by between-patient differences in interpersonal style (even among patients with similar symptom severity and presentation).

text.text: In line with this argument, several studies have shown that interpersonal style can predict treatment process (in terms of therapeutic alliance development; Zilcha-Mano et al., 2015), which in turn has been shown to predict treatment success.

text.text: Indeed, interpersonal style is considered particularly relevant during patient-therapist interaction and can thus be targeted within the therapeutic context (e.g., Kiesler, 1996).

text.text: Consequently, pretreatment assessment of interpersonal style could be highly informative for clinical practice.
There have been systematic reviews of IIP studies conducted in patients with mental disorders (Gómez Penedo and Flückiger, 2023; Gómez Penedo et al., 2025b; McFarquhar et al., 2018).

text.text: These reviews mostly focused on IIP-derived general interpersonal distress.
One review included a metaanalysis that showed a moderate to large decrease in interpersonal distress with treatment (specifically, psychotherapy for depression; McFarquhar et al., 2018).

text.text: Higher pre-treatment interpersonal distress was again predictive of a worse treatment outcome, irrespective of the type of treatment (e.g., psychotherapy vs. medication).

While this review also found that pre-treatment communion and agency scores did not significantly predict treatment outcome, these scores were considered separately, rather than as a blend representing interpersonal style.

Overall, while the aforementioned reviews of IIP studies are valuable and provide clinically relevant insights, none of these reviews considered how patients with the same mental disorder but different interpersonal styles may vary in the presentation and course of their disorder.
The aim of the present study was to evaluate the currently available clinical data on interpersonal heterogeneity in mental disorders.

Accordingly, we present the results of a systematic review of studies that included individuals with a primary diagnosis of a mental disorder according to Axis I of the fourth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM; American Psychiatric Association, 1994) or comparable (e.g., DSM-5, International Classification of Diseases; American Psychiatric Association, 2013; World Health Organization, 2010) and that used a version of the IIP (for a scoping review, see Hughes and Barkham, 2005) to derive subgroups characterized by different interpersonal styles.

text.text: Our first research question was: What interpersonal subgroups can be identified among individuals diagnosed with a mental disorder?
We expected to find subgroups across all quadrants of the interpersonal circumplex model, regardless of diagnoses.
This would serve to show that there is no one-to-one relation between a specific interpersonal style and a specific mental disorder, thus supporting the transdiagnostic utility of CIIT.
The existence of subgroups also provides necessary evidence for interpersonal pathoplasticity (Cain et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The existence of subgroups also provides necessary evidence for interpersonal pathoplasticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cain et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Our second research question was: How do interpersonal styles relate to the presentation and course of mental disorder?

In support of interpersonal pathoplasticity, interpersonal subgroups were not expected to differ on demographic variables, nor on clinical presentation at the time of diagnosis (e.g., pre-treatment symptom levels and general interpersonal distress; Cain et al., 2010).

text.text: At the same time, interpersonal subgroups were expected to differ on longitudinal outcomes.
This would also be consistent with the criteria for interpersonal pathoplasticity (Wright et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This would also be consistent with the criteria for interpersonal pathoplasticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wright et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the rationale for our review was that the interpersonal style of patients with a mental disorder may moderate their clinical outcome (e.g., Cain et al., 2010).

text.text: Evidence for this could be used to inform and improve the process and content of treatment across psychiatric diagnoses.

While a transdiagnostic approach to the treatment of mental disorders has been developing in recent years (Dalgleish et al., 2020; Farchione et al., 2024), to date this approach has mostly targeted behaviours, cognitions, and emotion regulation without an explicit focus on interpersonal situations.

text.text: The review was preregistered on Prospero (#56229).
Two deviations from the preregistration should be noted.
Firstly, we also included studies in which less than 100%, but still more than 50%, of participants had a primary diagnosis of a DSM-IV Axis I mental disorder or comparable.
Second, we included studies in which patients had a variety of diagnoses on Axis I and sometimes on Axis II.
This was considered acceptable provided most patients had an Axis I disorder.
We first searched PsycInfo and Medline on 16 October 2024, using EBSCOhost.
Our specific search string is available in the Supplementary Material.

We preregistered the following selection criteria: (a) Studies were empirical, cross-sectional or longitudinal, peer reviewed, and published as an academic journal article, with no restrictions to the date or language of publication.
Studies in books or dissertations, case studies, and unpublished studies were excluded.

(b) Study samples consisted of adults with a primary diagnosis of a DSM-IV Axis I mental disorder or comparable, excluding (neuro)cognitive disorders, sexual or gender identity disorders, sleep disorders, somatoform disorders, adjustment disorders, and disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence.
Samples (primarily) consisting of adults with a primary diagnosis of a DSM-IV Axis II personality disorder or comparable were also excluded.
If patients <18 years of age were included, then the mean age of the sample was at least 18 years.

text.text: Two independent raters (A2 and A3 -BLINDED FOR REVIEW) screened all articles using the title and abstract.

Due to moderate agreement (Cohen's kappa = .54), articles on which the two raters disagreed were generally retained, to reduce the risk of inadvertently excluding relevant articles before reading the full text.
The same raters then independently assessed the full text of the remaining articles for eligibility, with substantial agreement, Cohen's kappa = .74.
In case of disagreement, articles were discussed between the two raters and, if needed, the first author was consulted.
Reasons for exclusion were noted according to the aforementioned selection criteria.

Most also found no significant differences in gender, except Q4 subgroups had a higher proportion of female participants than Q3 subgroups in some studies (Clapp et al., 2014; Grosse Holtforth et al., 2014; Locke et al., 2018; Simon et al., 2015), suggesting that women were somewhat more likely than men to have a warm-submissive interpersonal style.

Overall, gender appeared the most likely to confound subgroup differences in clinical variables, but at the same time only a few studies considered or formally analysed subgroup differences in demographic variables.

text.text: The follow-up period in the study by Gómez Penedo et al. (2019) was 4 sessions, and in the remaining three studies it was 6 months.
Overall, 11 out of the 19 reviewed studies included findings on subgroup differences in treatment process and/or outcome.
Three studies that included treatment process measures found evidence for better therapeutic alliance development among Q4 subgroups.
Four studies that included treatment outcome measures found larger decreases in interpersonal distress or symptom severity among Q4 subgroups.
Subgroup Q4 thus compared favourably to the other subgroups.
While this was not found in all longitudinal studies, no study found better outcomes in other subgroups.

text.text: Most studies had clear selection criteria, adequately described sample characteristics and setting, included psychometric data on the IIP, and specified how interpersonal subgroups were identified.
Studies were more variable on the other quality assessment criteria.

In particular, demographic differences between subgroups were not always examined and, if present, dealt with strategically, and most longitudinal studies were unclear or did not adequately present the methods and validity of longitudinal outcomes.
Besides, some studies met fewer quality assessment criteria than others.
In this systematic review, we answered two research questions aiming to evaluate the currently available clinical data on interpersonal heterogeneity among patients with mental disorders.
Our first question was on the existence of different interpersonal subgroups.
To answer this question, we reviewed studies of individuals with a DSM-IV Axis I mental disorder (or comparable) that identified interpersonal subgroups using the IIP.
As expected, we found subgroups in all four quadrants of the interpersonal space, indicating that interpersonal style can vary substantially, both within psychiatric diagnoses and across.
This supports more frequent inclusion of the IIP during pre-treatment clinical assessment.
The IIP has mostly been used to assess patients' overall level of interpersonal distress, but it can also give insight into which specific behaviours are likely to contribute to the distress.

As such, even though the IIP says little about the overall quality of a patient's social relationships, it can help explain what types of problems patients may experience in personally relevant interpersonal situations, including in daily life (e.g., with romantic partners) but also in therapy (with clinicians).
While the finding of interpersonal heterogeneity in mental disorders is not new, our review highlights its occurrence across diagnoses and thereby the transdiagnostic value of the IIP.

While we found interpersonal subgroups across all four quadrants of the interpersonal circumplex model, subgroups in the two submissive quadrants (Q3 and Q4 in Figure 1) were more common than subgroups in the dominant quadrants (Q1 and Q2).

text.text: Overall, across diagnostic categories, we found evidence in line with the broader differentiation between internalising and externalising disorders, but also evidence indicating that not all patients with an internalising disorder (e.g., anxiety, depression) versus an externalising disorder (e.g., cocaine dependence) fit this type of differentiation, or can be differentiated along the dimensions of agency alone.
Overall, interpersonal heterogeneity was clearly present.
In relation to our second research question, we were primarily expecting to find differences in the course of mental disorder, regardless of demographic variables and clinical presentation.
The 11 studies that had a longitudinal component all focused on treatment (Table 3).

text.text: Three studies examined a treatment process measure, namely, therapeutic alliance during the initial sessions or weeks.
In all three studies, warm-submissive subgroups had a more favourable treatment process than other subgroups.

These findings align with other studies showing better alliance development among patients with higher levels of communion (Altenstein-Yamanaka et al., 2017; Dinger et al., 2013; Kushner et al., 2016), lower levels of agency (Gómez Penedo et al., 2020; Renner et al., 2012), or both (i.e., more friendly submissiveness; Constantino and Smith-Hansen, 2008).

text.text: Seven of the longitudinal studies examined decreases in symptom severity or general interpersonal distress as treatment outcome measures.

In four of these studies, warm-submissive subgroups tended to have better treatment outcomes than cold-submissive or cold-dominant subgroups, most notably larger decreases in general interpersonal distress.
The follow-up period was 6 months in the three of the four studies.
The studies that considered the same outcome measures, but did not find subgroup differences, were comparable in length.
The observed subgroup differences in treatment process and outcome were found in nearabsence of differences in demographics and pre-treatment clinical presentation (Table 2).

text.text: Thus, subgroup differences in treatment success could not readily be explained by these variables, at least not at the group level and within one diagnostic category.
Nonetheless, it may be premature to rule out their confounding influence.

Subgroup differences in demographic and pre-treatment clinical variables, including general interpersonal distress, were often not evaluated systematically, or perhaps not found due to sample size or limited sample variability (e.g., in ethnicity or education).

It remains possible that demographic variables such as gender, and clinical variables such as pretreatment interpersonal distress, are significant contributors to observed subgroup differences in longitudinal outcomes.

If warm-submissive patients have a higher rate of treatment success than cold-submissive patients (who formed the second most common subgroup across the reviewed studies), and if developing an alliance with cold-submissive patients is more difficult, then perhaps an increased focus on alliance development in cold-submissive patients could be beneficial.
This could be achieved by assigning cold-submissive patients to a more intensive treatment (Zevalkink and Berghout, 2008) and perhaps also by being a more empathetic therapist (Cain et al., 2010).

text.text: Additionally, the treatment of coldsubmissive patients could be tailored such that they learn to become more communal.

For example, a focus on fear of negative evaluation, aiming to reduce social avoidance, has been proposed for cold-submissive patients with social phobia (Cain et al., 2010) but may also benefit cold-submissive patients with another primary diagnosis, such as persistent depressive disorder (where coldsubmissiveness is relatively common; Ley et al., 2011).

text.text: At a broader level, our results suggest that distinct mental disorders, as diagnosed using the DSM or comparable, can have comparable interpersonal correlates.

This highlights the need for transdiagnostic research on how interpersonal style relates to the core emotional and cognitive symptoms of mental disorders (e.g., feeling tense or sad, negative thinking patterns) rather than to the diagnoses per se (Girard et al., 2017).

text.text: Moreover, while our results do not provide direct evidence for interpersonal pathoplasticity, they align with the concept.
We distinguish between limitations of the studies included in our review, and of the review itself.

Regarding the former, while we conducted an extensive quality assessment and found study quality to be generally acceptable, few studies clearly described relevant demographic and pre-treatment clinical variables in detail.
Moreover, even when such variables were available, few studies formally compared subgroups on these variables, or fully reported these comparisons, as mentioned earlier.
Most reviewed studies used cluster analysis to derive subgroups.
In general, the value of such a categorical approach to characterize interpersonal problems has been criticised (Wendt et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In general, the value of such a categorical approach to characterize interpersonal problems has been criticised <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Wendt et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, reviewed studies that used cluster analysis (or latent class analysis or latent profile analysis) generally assumed at least two subgroups and varied in the maximum number of subgroups assumed.
Such methodological variations reduced the comparability of the results across studies.
Besides, results derived from cluster analysis may depend on the characteristics and size of the sample being studied (König et al., 2016).

text.text: Reassuringly, we found a reasonably clear pattern favouring warm-submissive subgroups in terms of treatment process and outcome, using a procedure that involved comparing subgroups by quadrant of the interpersonal circumplex model.
Nonetheless, this quadrant-based approach was neither preregistered nor without drawbacks.
Several studies had multiple subgroups in Q3 or Q4, see Table S2, and sometimes there were differences between subgroups in the same quadrant, see Tables 2 and 3.

Our review focused on studies conducted in patients with DSM-IV Axis I mental disorders (or comparable) that used the IIP to divide samples into interpersonal subgroups.

text.text: As these findings are in line with those of our review, we believe that including studies that used non-clinical samples or questionnaires other than the IIP would not have altered our results and conclusions.
Nonetheless, questionnaires in general are limited by being self-evaluative measures.
Additional research on interpersonal styles defined by other types of measures (e.g., observational or implicit measures) would be expected to generate additional insights.

text.text: More broadly, we support a transdiagnostic approach to examine if interpersonal heterogeneity has value in understanding the presentation and course of psychopathology.
Most individual studies included in this review focused on one diagnosis.

On the one hand, meaningful subgroup differences in clinical variables such as pre-treatment symptom severity and general interpersonal distress may emerge when multiple mental disorders are considered simultaneously.
Such cross-sectional subgroup differences would confound evidence of subgroup differences in longitudinal outcomes and thereby challenge the concept of interpersonal pathoplasticity.

On the other hand, if interpersonal heterogeneity were found to have explanatory and prognostic value beyond psychiatric diagnoses, this could have a significant impact on research and clinical practice.
If future research continues to find that interpersonal style relates to the course of mental disorder, then the practical use of measures such as the IIP becomes even more clinically relevant.
To date, the IIP has mostly been used to track changes in general interpersonal distress in the context of treatment (e.g., McFarquhar et al., 2018).

text.text: Furthermore, pre-treatment assessment of an individual patient's interpersonal style may inform therapists not only on what to expect during their interactions with the patient (e.g., Kiesler, 1996) but also on how to tailor treatment to the patient, for example, by offering assertiveness training to Q3/Q4 but not Q2/Q1 patients.

text.text: This more personalized approach could be expected to contribute to a change in the patient's style, which in turn could help prevent the re-emergence of interpersonal distress and mental disorder.
This idea deserves further study but is broadly in line with other recent literature on the relevance of CIIT for psychotherapy (Cain et al., 2024; Pincus and Hopwood, 2025).

text.text: Clinically, we believe the quadrant-based approach to be both intuitive and practical.
Each patient can easily be placed in the quadrant corresponding to their IIP-derived angular displacement score.
This provides immediate insight into the nature of their interpersonal problems, along the dimensions of communion and agency, and may even have predictive value for treatment success.
This systematic review found that interpersonal subgroups characterized by warm-dominance, colddominance, cold-submissiveness, and warm-submissiveness can be found across diagnostic categories.

More importantly, we synthesized evidence in support of the notion that patients with anxiety, mood, and substance-related disorders may have a more favourable treatment process and outcome if they have a warm-submissive interpersonal style.
Accordingly, the disorder may be less important than the (interpersonal style of) the patient that is being treated.

Appendix 1) Selection criteria: This criterion assesses the clarity with which inclusion criteria are described.

"Yes" is assigned when the selection criteria are clear and explicitly stated, "Unclear" is assigned when the selection criteria are vaguely defined, and "No" is assigned when selection criteria are absent.

2) Sample characteristics and setting: This criterion evaluates a) the clarity with which the clinical characteristics of participants and the clinical setting are described, and b) whether demographic information (gender/sex and age) is reported.

"Yes" is assigned if both clinical characteristics and setting, as well as demographic characteristics, are clearly described, "Unclear" is assigned if one of the two components is missing, and "No" is assigned when both components are absent.

3) IIP psychometrics: This criterion assesses whether the psychometric properties of the IIP are adequately described, regarding a) reliability, such that Cronbach's alpha (or an equivalent statistic) is reported for the current sample; and b) validity, such that either structural or construct validity is examined.

"Yes" is assigned when both reliability and validity are clearly reported, "Unclear" is assigned when one of the two components is rated "no" or when most information is unclear, and "No" is assigned when both components are rated "no".

4) Identifying interpersonal subgroups: This criterion evaluates the clarity with which interpersonal subgroups are derived, specifically: a) statistical analyses and software used, b) number of solutions explored and chosen, and c) clarity of the basis for analysis (e.g., agency and communion dimensions, ipsatized octant scores).

"Yes" is assigned when all three components are clearly described, "Unclear" is assigned when one subcriterion is rated "no" or one or more components are unclear, and "No" is assigned when two or more subcriteria are rated "no".

5) Demographic differences between interpersonal subgroups: This criterion assesses whether demographic factors, namely age and/or gender/sex, are considered as potential confounders, and whether subgroup differences relative to these demographics are examined.

"NA" is assigned when demographic differences were examined under Criterion 5 but none were found.
